title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti's proposal highlights water reuse, power strain and what it means for bills across the state.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're zeroing in on a Ypsilanti proposal that's putting water and power questions front and center for communities across the state.
Yeah, this feels like one of those moments where a single local plan could ripple out pretty far.
Exactly. Eastern Michigan University hydrogeologist Christopher Gellasch spoke at a presentation today explaining how closed-loop cooling systems can reuse groundwater without warming the subsurface.
That sounds promising on paper. How does that actually work in practice for these big facilities?

He laid it out as a way to minimize some of the usual groundwater concerns, but activist Peter Sinclair was also there pointing out that new energy infrastructure might still be needed as a community trade-off.
So even with reuse tech, we're still talking about major power demands that could affect the grid.

Right. And that's the bigger picture we're digging into tonight — how these projects land in places like Washtenaw County and what it could mean for electric bills, water supplies, and local planning everywhere from metro Detroit to western Michigan.
Walk me through the history here. How long has Michigan been seeing this kind of interest?

Interest has been building for a while, but it's really accelerated with AI demand. Today's Ypsilanti discussion is part of a wave of local officials trying to get ahead of applications before they hit the desk.
That makes sense. What are the main players in these conversations?

You've got hydrogeologists like Gellasch giving the technical side, activists like Sinclair raising the quality-of-life flags, and then state-level voices like the senator who flagged risks today and Attorney General Nessel pressing the PSC on Friday.
Nessel's move on Friday seems key. What exactly is she asking?

She's demanding the Public Service Commission justify how it's handling these surging electricity loads. The worry is residents end up subsidizing big new users through higher rates if oversight isn't tightened.
And that ties directly into what residents 30 miles away might feel, right?
Precisely. A facility in one township can push demand on the same DTE or Consumers grid that serves suburbs farther out.
What about water specifically? Beyond the closed-loop talk, what are the real strains?
Cooling these servers takes a lot, and the senator today warned that communities without strong local rules could see supplies stretched, especially in suburbs already eyeing growth.
And farmland or towns — how does that factor in?
Zoning fights are popping up because these sites need space, roads, and quiet. Pittsfield Township tightened its rules this week after residents raised noise and traffic alarms near Ann Arbor.
Noise is already a lived issue elsewhere, isn't it?
Yes — in Dowagiac, residents in Cass County have been complaining since Thursday that a facility runs nonstop and the sound carries constantly with no quick fix from officials.
That quality-of-life piece feels under-discussed compared to the utility bills.
It does, and it's why townships like the one in West Michigan got their first detailed look today at drafting ordinances on noise, roads, and power before any applications arrive.
So what's the timeline for these rules actually taking effect?
Most places are moving fast on drafting now, hoping to have something in place before developers show up with proposals.
What happens next if a township doesn't act quickly?
They risk being the ones absorbing the impacts without leverage — higher bills, strained water, or having to play catch-up on zoning like Detroit did after its assessment this week.
Detroit's draft rules include size limits and requiring developers to pay for upgrades, right?
That's the approach there — and it could become a model, though every community has its own grid realities to consider.
On the power side, Mason County was questioning its grid capacity on Friday. Any updates on that?
Residents there are still asking whether new plants or upgrades will be needed and who pays, especially with AI facilities potentially adding major load.
And then there's the on-site power pitch from a Michigan firm on Friday. How does that fit?
They say it can deliver the loads without waiting on utility upgrades, which might speed things up but raises fresh questions on emissions and noise.
Cybersecurity popped up too with the OpenAI offer after the water system hack. What's the connection?
The hack hit utilities already under strain from data-center demands, so hardening those systems matters for any new clusters that rely on the same infrastructure.
Overall, it feels like the state is at a decision point on how tightly to regulate this growth.
It does. Local rules, state oversight, and tech solutions like closed-loop cooling are all on the table, but the outcomes will depend on how quickly communities move.
And for listeners 30 or 60 miles from any proposed site, why should they care today?
Because the grid and water systems are shared. One big load in Ypsilanti or Mason County can influence rates and reliability for a much wider area if not managed.
What's your sense of where this lands in the next few weeks?
More townships will likely hold presentations like today's, and we'll see if the AG's pressure leads to stronger PSC guidelines.
Thanks for laying that out so clearly.
Let's shift to the other stories making news this week.
Starting with the West Michigan township that got its first look today at noise, power, and water rules for potential server farms.
Officials there heard how large facilities could affect roads and electric demand, and they're drafting ordinances now to get ahead of any applications.
Next up, that state senator alerting locals about power and water risks in suburbs without strong rules.
She's warning that communities could end up subsidizing data centers through higher utility bills if they don't act on zoning and oversight.
On Friday, Mason County residents questioned whether the local grid can handle the surge from AI proposals.
They're asking about new power plants or upgrades and who pays to avoid blackouts or rate hikes.
Attorney General Nessel also pressed the PSC on Friday about handling these big new loads.
She's seeking justification for how demand is managed so residents aren't left with the bill.
OpenAI offered help on cybersecurity for water utilities after a recent hack tied to data-center growth.
The offer targets vulnerabilities in systems already strained by AI demands.
A local firm pitched on-site power on Friday as a way around grid delays.
It could accelerate projects but brings up emissions and who covers the costs when the grid is tight.
Detroit released its assessment and draft rules this week after flagging hundreds of megawatts of new demand.
The rules would limit sizes and make developers pay for upgrades to protect suburban ratepayers.
Dowagiac residents have been dealing with nonstop noise from an existing facility since at least Thursday.
Local officials have no immediate fix, so homeowners are left absorbing the impact.
And Pittsfield Township moved this week to tighten zoning near Ann Arbor.
The changes target noise, traffic, and power concerns and could influence other Washtenaw County townships.
No major public meetings listed for this weekend on the tracker.
That's right — but township boards across the state are expected to keep reviewing ordinances in the coming days.
Listeners should check their local agendas for any data-center related items popping up mid-week.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Data Center Plan Spotlights Water and Power Tradeoffs for Michigan Towns
